bill.title: To clarify the Holocaust Expropriated Art Recovery Act of 2016, to appropriately limit the application of defenses based on the passage of time and other non-merits defenses to claims under that Act.
bill.latestActionText: Referred to the House Committee on the Judiciary.
subjects: War crimes, genocide, crimes against humanity
bill.officialSummary: This bill permanently extends and expands judicial authority under the Holocaust Expropriated Art Recovery Act of 2016. The law allows and establishes procedures for civil claims and causes of action to recover artwork and other property lost between 1933 and 1945 because of Nazi persecution. Among the changes, the bill removes the deadline for filing civil claims or causes of action. Currently, the filing deadline is December 31, 2026. (Claims must still be filed within six years of the claimant's discovery of the property in question.) The bill permits courts to exercise jurisdiction over civil claims or causes of action against a foreign state without regard to the nationality or citizenship of the alleged victim. The art or property at issue must still have a connection to the foreign state's commercial activities in the United States. Additionally, the bill authorizes nationwide service of process, which allows courts to exercise personal jurisdiction over defendants in any judicial district where they may be found, reside, have an agent, or transact business. Finally, the bill limits the defenses that may be asserted against civil claims or causes of action, including by prohibiting defenses based on the passage of time, including equitable defenses such as laches (i.e., unreasonable delays); and discretionary bases for dismissal that are unrelated to the merits of the claim, including international comity (i.e., deference to the laws of other countries). These changes apply to pending and future civil claims or causes of action.

classification.plainSummary: This bill removes the 2026 deadline for filing lawsuits to recover art and property stolen during the Holocaust, allowing claims to be filed indefinitely as long as they are brought within six years of discovering the item. It makes it easier to sue foreign governments in U.S. courts and to serve legal papers on defendants anywhere in the country. The bill also blocks certain legal defenses, such as arguments that too much time has passed or that U.S. courts should defer to foreign laws, for both current and future cases.

industries.rationale: The bill expands litigation procedures, jurisdictional reach, and limits defenses in civil claims, directly affecting law firms handling art recovery and international litigation.
Museums and cultural institutions holding artwork are subject to expanded liability and jurisdictional reach under the modified claims procedures.

plain.whatItDoes: This bill permanently would extend and widen judicial authority under the Holocaust Expropriated Art Recovery Act of 2016.
plain.whoItTouches: People who have been the victim of a crime.
plain.everydayEffect: If it passed, the change would show up in what help you can get. Nothing has changed yet. Most bills never become law.

disclaimer: This tool places two public records next to each other: who donated to a member of Congress, and what that member legislated on. Any overlap you see is a correlation, not causation. It is not evidence of a quid pro quo, of influence, or of wrongdoing. Legislators routinely receive support from industries in their district for the same reason they legislate on them: those industries are there.
